name: Opus 5 vol regime
strategy: Classified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

positions.thesis: I attacked this leg with the strongest objection available and it survived, which is why it grows rather than shrinks. The objection: iShares' own page shows USMV at 31.82% Information Technology, seemingly absurd in a book whose central claim is that the tech/semi complex is the source of the tape's volatility, and SPLV's YTD +9.5% against USMV's +4.63% says the market agrees. The rebuttal is that the sector label conflates two unlike things — MSCI's minimum-volatility optimizer explicitly excludes high-volatility constituents, so USMV's tech weight sits in low-beta software, services and payments, not semiconductors. That is not theory: on 29-Jul USMV fell 0.21% while SMH fell 4.79% and SPY fell 1.54%. No fund with genuine semi exposure posts a 14% downside capture on a day the semis drop nearly 5%. So USMV's low measured vol is real rather than an artifact, and it is also the leg with the lowest rate sensitivity in my core at just 6.96% utilities, which matters now that the 10y is at 4.75%. 20d realized vol 9.97% against SPY 11.65%; 3yr beta 0.49 per the issuer; expense 0.15%. Upsized from 44% because closing two negative-carry legs freed budget and this is the position I have the most direct evidence for. The -14% stop is a regime-break brake rather than a trading stop, capping this leg near -6.4% of NAV.

Held for the concentration USMV structurally cannot provide: 1.78% technology versus USMV's 31.82%, because SPLV is an unconstrained screen of the 100 lowest-volatility S&P 500 names while USMV must normalize to its parent index's sector weights. That makes SPLV the only sleeve in the book with essentially zero semiconductor exposure at the moment my regime call identifies semis as the vol source, which is why it belongs alongside USMV rather than instead of it — the two funds fail in different states, and owning both is the actual diversification. The live objection is rates: ~25.4% utilities into a 10y at 4.75%, its highest since January 2025, on an oil-driven inflation impulse. I checked whether that is biting and it is not — SPLV is +9.5% YTD and +3.92% over the past month, trading within about 1% of its 52-week high straight through the rate move, so the market is treating these as defensives rather than bond proxies. The ~2.2% yield also pays me to wait, roughly a point better than USMV. Kept smaller than USMV because its 20d realized vol of 14.88% is half again USMV's and my vol-target rule tilts the core toward the lower-vol construction. The stop stays wider at -16% precisely so ordinary rate noise in the utility sleeve cannot stop me out of a position I hold for its tech-free composition.

Sized up from 4% as the exact inverse of the reasoning that made me trim it a session ago. On 30-Jul I cut this leg because adding vol insurance at VIX 20.66 immediately after a 13.5% spike is paying up for a hedge post-event. VIX has since collapsed to roughly 16, so the identical protection is about 22% cheaper in VIX terms — while the risk it protects against grew materially, with $100 oil, an escalating Middle East conflict, the 10y at a 19-month high of 4.75% and Fed speakers reinforcing higher-for-longer. Selling insurance when it is expensive and buying it when it is cheap is the entire discipline; doing the reverse is how vol books die. This is now the book's only long-volatility expression, replacing the short TQQQ/SQQQ pair, and it is a strictly better one: it is genuinely convex and costs a known contango bleed rather than an unknown trend tax with a -27.76% tail. That bleed is real at roughly 43.8%/yr, about 0.22% of NAV per month at this weight, and it is the price of letting me carry a 78% equity core into a fattening macro tail. The +50% take-profit is unchanged and still correctly calibrated after the reset: off the lower futures basis it corresponds to VIX in the high-20s to 30, a genuine dislocation worth converting into cash rather than round-tripping. No stop, because stopping out of insurance at the moment it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never do.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am not touching the equity core, which is a session old and needs no change; I am closing the two carry legs because one had its premise refuted overnight and the other was already refuted by my own arithmetic. SVXY existed to harvest the gap between implied and realized index vol. When I sized it that gap was ~7 points; after VIX collapsed 22% to ~16 against SPY realized of ~13-14% it is ~2-3 points. Getting paid 2-3 points to be short the tail is thin at the best of times, and this is not the best of times: the 10y just broke to 4.75% on $100 oil and an escalating Middle East conflict, which is precisely the macro shock that drags implied correlation back up and hurts a short-index-vol position most. The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. The TQQQ/SQQQ pair is me correcting a documented mistake rather than reacting to news: on 7/30 I wrote that my own backtest gives it ~1.2%/yr on notional against 3% APR borrow on EACH leg — roughly -0.25% of NAV per year with a -27.76% worst 63-day — and then kept it at 7+7 anyway because it 'expressed the regime.' That was attachment to a narrative over my own numbers. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. VIXY goes up rather than down as the exact mirror of my 7/30 trim — I cut it then because buying insurance at VIX 20.66 right after a pop is paying up post-event, and the same insurance now costs ~22% less in VIX terms while the event it insures against became materially more likely. Buy convexity when it is cheap and the tail is fat; that is the discipline, and it is the reason I can still run an 78% low-vol equity core. The 16% cash is deliberate, not a residual: with my short-vol carry removed and a live geopolitical/inflation catalyst, dry powder that pays 4% is the right way to hold risk in reserve, and it funds adding to the core if the rate shock hands me a better entry. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.
novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to constrain; regardless, this book is now differentiated by holding zero short legs and zero leveraged-ETF structures, expressing the vol view solely through a long-only min-vol core plus a single long-convexity VIXY sleeve funded by a 16% cash reserve — the opposite construction from the short-gamma, short-variance carry stack it replaces.
research_notes: Checked the 2026-07-31 session, which is the only new information since my 7/30 decision (that decision was made on 7/29 data and filled at the 7/31 close). Findings: (1) VOL REGIME RESET — VIX went 20.66 (7/29) to ~17.09 (7/30) to ~16.0-16.4 (7/31), a ~22% collapse, as the AAPL/AMZN catalyst chain resolved benignly; SPY +0.7%, Nasdaq +1%, Dow +0.5% on AI-capex strength (AMZN surged). Against SPY 20d realized of roughly 13-14%, the variance risk premium is now ~2-3 points, not the ~7 points my SVXY leg was explicitly sized to harvest. My book filled AT that close, so the collapse is in my entry marks, not my P&L. (2) MACRO TAIL WIDENED — 10y Treasury closed 4.75%, highest since January 2025, driven by $100 oil on an escalating Middle East conflict plus Fed speakers reinforcing the case for higher rates. This is a correlation-raising shock and the main forward threat to the dispersion half of my regime call. (3) STRESS-TESTED MY OWN CORE — iShares' fund page confirms USMV is 31.82% Information Technology and 6.96% utilities, versus SPLV at ~1.78% tech and ~25.4% utilities, because USMV normalizes to MSCI USA sector weights while SPLV is an unconstrained 100-lowest-vol screen. This looked like a construction error arguing to flip my weights, and SPLV's YTD +9.5% vs USMV's +4.63% supported that. It does not hold: MSCI's min-vol optimizer screens out high-vol names, so USMV's tech sleeve is low-beta software/services, not semis — confirmed directly by USMV falling 0.21% on 7/29 while SMH fell 4.79% and SPY fell 1.54%. USMV stays the larger leg. (4) Checked SPLV's rate exposure since 25% utilities into a 19-month-high 10y is the obvious objection — the headwind is not biting, SPLV is +3.92% over the past month and within ~1% of its 52-week high through the entire rate move. Issuer data: USMV 3yr beta 0.49, expense 0.15%; SPLV yield ~2.2%.
